primary.key: The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this.
primary.s: After the Duke of Sheh praises a son who testifies that his father stole a sheep, Confucius answers him; Zhu Xi, on 13.18, reads father and son shielding each other as the utmost of heavenly principle and human feeling, in which uprightness comes unsought.
primary.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 13.18, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, Lunyu jizhu juan 7), revision 2412885 (2024)

basis.words: 父子相隱，天理人情之至也。故不求為直，而直在其中。
basis.gloss: When father and son conceal each other’s faults, that is the utmost of heavenly principle and human feeling. So they do not seek to be upright, and yet uprightness is found in it.

standby.key: The Master said, ‘The superior man is affable, but not adulatory; the mean man is adulatory, but not affable.’
standby.s: This is one of Book 13’s contrasts between two kinds of men; He Yan, in his own note on 13.23, reads the first as harmonious in heart though each sees differently, the second as alike in tastes but contending for profit.
standby.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, own note on 13.23, zh.wikisource (the jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 13), revision 2371796 (2024)

basis.words: 君子心和，然其所見各異，故曰不同。小人所嗜好者同，然各爭利，故曰不和。
basis.gloss: The superior man is harmonious in heart, yet what each one sees differs; so it says ‘not the same’. What mean men like and relish is the same, yet each contends for profit; so it says ‘not harmonious’.

primary.key: The Master said, ‘He who speaks without modesty will find it difficult to make his words good.’
primary.s: After judgements on princes and their ministers, the day’s passage closes on a saying about speech; He Yan’s collection, on 14.21, gives Ma Rong, who reads unashamed speech as coming from substance within, and the gathering of that substance as what is hard.
primary.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, Ma Rong’s gloss on 14.21, zh.wikisource (the jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 14), revision 2371072 (2024)

basis.words: 馬曰：“怍，慚也。內有其實，則言之不慚。積其實者，為之難。”
basis.gloss: Ma Rong says: zuo means to be ashamed. If one has the reality within, one speaks of it without shame. The gathering of that reality is what is hard to do.

standby.key: The Master said, ‘This may be regarded as the achievement of what is difficult. But I do not know that it is to be deemed perfect virtue.’
standby.s: Told that holding down four faults, boasting and covetousness among them, counts as perfect virtue, the Master answers; Zhu Xi, on 14.2, reads the curbing as hard, but perfect virtue as heavenly principle entire, of itself free of the four.
standby.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 14.2, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, Lunyu jizhu juan 7), revision 2412885 (2024)

basis.words: 有是四者而能制之，使不得行，可謂難矣。仁則天理渾然，自無四者之累，不行不足以言之也。
basis.gloss: To have these four and be able to control them so that they cannot act may be called difficult. But perfect virtue is heavenly principle whole and entire, of itself free of the burden of the four; ‘not acting’ is not enough to describe it.

primary.key: ‘Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness.’
primary.s: Asked about repaying injury with kindness, the Master asks what would then repay kindness; Zhu Xi, on 14.36, reads justice here as love and hate, taking and refusing, all ruled by utmost fairness without self-interest, and kindness received as never to be forgotten.
primary.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 14.36, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, Lunyu jizhu juan 7), revision 2412885 (2024)

basis.words: 於其所怨者，愛憎取捨，一以至公而無私，所謂直也。於其所德者，則必以德報之，不可忘也。
basis.gloss: Towards one who has wronged him, his loving and hating, taking and rejecting, are all by utmost impartiality with nothing private: this is what is called uprightness (Legge’s justice). Towards one who has shown him kindness, he must repay it with kindness and may not forget it.

standby.key: My studies lie low, and my penetration rises high.
standby.s: Pressed by Tsze-kung after lamenting that no one knows him, the Master blames neither Heaven nor men; He Yan’s collection, on 14.37, gives Kong Anguo, who reads the low studies as human affairs and the high reach as knowing the decree of Heaven.
standby.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, Kong Anguo’s gloss on 14.37, zh.wikisource (the jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 14), revision 2371072 (2024)

basis.words: 孔曰：“下學人事，上知天命。”
basis.gloss: Kong Anguo says: below, he learns human affairs; above, he comes to know the decree of Heaven.

primary.key: ‘No,’ was the answer; ‘I seek a unity all-pervading.’
primary.s: The Master asks Tsze-kung whether he takes him for a man of wide learning and memory; He Yan, in his own note on 15.2, reads the unity as knowing the origin of every good, so that all are known through one, without much learning.
primary.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, own note on 15.2, zh.wikisource (the jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 15), revision 7904695 (2026)

basis.words: 善有元，事有會，天下殊塗而同歸，百慮而一致。知其元則眾善舉矣，故不待多學而一知之。
basis.gloss: Good has its origin and affairs their meeting point; all under heaven reach the same end by different roads, and one conclusion through a hundred thoughts. Know the origin, and all the many goods are raised; so he does not wait on much learning, but knows them by the one.

standby.key: The Master said, ‘A man can enlarge the principles which he follows; those principles do not enlarge the man.’
standby.s: Among sayings on conduct and learning, the Master speaks of man and his path; Zhu Xi, on 15.28, reads the principles as the Way, which in itself does nothing while man’s mind is aware, so man can enlarge it and it cannot enlarge him.
standby.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 15.28, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, Lunyu jizhu juan 8), revision 2304542 (2023)

basis.words: 人外無道，道外無人。然人心有覺，而道體無為；故人能大其道，道不能大其人也。
basis.gloss: Outside man there is no Way, and outside the Way there is no man. Yet the human mind is aware, while the Way in its substance does nothing; so man can make the Way great, and the Way cannot make man great.

primary.key: ‘When right principles prevail in the kingdom, there will be no discussions among the common people.’
primary.s: Confucius traces authority slipping from the son of Heaven down to retainers, then turns to the common people; Zhu Xi, on 16.2, reads it as no private criticism below when government above does not fail, not as mouths gagged into silence.
primary.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 16.2, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, Lunyu jizhu juan 8), revision 2304542 (2023)

basis.words: 上無失政，則下無私議。非箝其口使不敢言也。
basis.gloss: When those above make no failure of government, those below have no private criticism. It is not that their mouths are clamped so that they dare not speak.

standby.key: He stands in awe of the ordinances of Heaven.
standby.s: Among the book’s sayings built on threes, Confucius names three objects of awe, the first given here; He Yan, in his own note on 16.8, reads Heaven’s ordinances as its decree that compliance brings good fortune and defiance brings ill.
standby.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, own note on 16.8, zh.wikisource (the jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 16), revision 2268333 (2023)

basis.words: 順吉逆凶，天之命也。…恢疏，故不知畏。
basis.gloss: To comply brings good fortune and to oppose brings misfortune: this is the decree (ordinance) of Heaven. … [On the mean man who does not know the ordinances of Heaven:] being lax and careless, he does not know to stand in awe.

primary.key: ‘Am I a bitter gourd! How can I be hung up out of the way of being eaten?’
primary.s: Invited by the rebel Pi Hsi, the Master answers Tsze-lu’s protest; He Yan, in his own note on 17.7, reads the gourd as hung in one place because it does not eat, whereas the Master, who eats, must go in every direction.
primary.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, own note on 17.7, zh.wikisource (the jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 17), revision 432755 (2015)

basis.words: 匏，瓠也。言瓠瓜得係一處者，不食故也。吾自食物，當東西南北，不得如不食之物，係滯一處。
basis.gloss: Pao is a gourd. It means that a gourd can be tied up in one place because it does not eat. I myself am a thing that eats, and must go east, west, south and north; I cannot be like a thing that does not eat, tied and held fast in one place.

standby.key: The Master said, ‘By nature, men are nearly alike; by practice, they get to be wide apart.’
standby.s: The Master speaks of how men come to differ, just before naming those who cannot change; Zhu Xi, on 17.2, reads this nature as including the physical endowment, which varies yet starts close, men drawing apart only as they practise good or evil.
standby.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 17.2, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, Lunyu jizhu juan 9), revision 2560458 (2025)

basis.words: 此所謂性，兼氣質而言者也。氣質之性，固有美惡之不同矣。然以其初而言，則皆不甚相遠也。但習於善則善，習於惡則惡，於是始相遠耳。
basis.gloss: The nature spoken of here is spoken of together with the physical endowment. The nature of the physical endowment certainly differs in fineness and fault; but taken at the beginning, none are very far apart. Only, practising good one becomes good, practising evil one becomes evil, and then they begin to be far apart.
